{{Short description|Complex-valued function}}
The '''Mehler kernel''' is a complex-valued function found to be the [[propagator]] of the [[quantum harmonic oscillator]].

It was first discovered by [[Gustav Ferdinand Mehler|Mehler]] in 1866, and since then, as [[Einar Hille]] remarked in 1932, "has been rediscovered by almost everybody who has worked in this field".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hardy |first=G. H. |date=1932-07-01 |title=Addendum: Summation of a Series of Polynomials of Laguerre* |url=https://academic.oup.com/jlms/article/s1-7/3/192/960574 |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |volume=s1-7 |issue=3 |pages=192 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-7.3.192-s |issn=0024-6107}}</ref>

== Mehler's formula ==
{{harvs|txt|last=Mehler|authorlink=Gustav Ferdinand Mehler|year=1866}} defined a function<ref>{{Citation | last1=Mehler | first1=F. G. | title=Ueber die Entwicklung einer Function von beliebig vielen Variabeln nach Laplaceschen Functionen höherer Ordnung | url=http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002152975 | language=German |id={{ERAM|066.1720cj}} | year=1866 | journal=Journal für die Reine und Angewandte Mathematik | issn=0075-4102 | issue=66 | pages=161–176}} (cf.  p 174, eqn (18)  & p 173, eqn (13) )</ref>
{{Equation box 1
|indent =::
|equation =  <math>E(x,y) =\frac 1{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\rho^2 (x^2+y^2)- 2\rho xy}{(1-\rho^2)}\right)~, </math>
|border
|border colour = #0073CF
|bgcolor=#F9FFF7}}
and showed, in modernized notation,<ref>{{citation|first1=Arthur|last1= Erdélyi|authorlink1=Arthur Erdélyi|first2= Wilhelm |last2=Magnus|authorlink2=Wilhelm Magnus|first3= Fritz|last3= Oberhettinger|first4=Francesco G.|last4= Tricomi|authorlink4=Francesco Tricomi|title= Higher transcendental functions. Vol. II|publisher= McGraw-Hill| year=1955}} ([http://www.nr.com/legacybooks scan]:  &nbsp;    [http://apps.nrbook.com/bateman/Vol2.pdf p.194 10.13 (22)])</ref> that it can be expanded in terms of [[Hermite polynomials]] <math>H(\cdot)</math> based on weight function <math>\exp(-x^2)</math> as
<math display="block">E(x,y) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(\rho/2)^n}{n!} ~ \mathit{H}_n(x)\mathit{H}_n(y) ~.</math>

This result is useful, in modified form, in quantum physics, [[probability theory]], and harmonic analysis. Equivalently, in the probabilist's Hermite polynomials:<math display="block">\frac 1{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\rho^2 \left(x^2+y^2\right) - 2\rho xy}{2\left(1-\rho^2\right)}\right)
 = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\rho^n}{n!} ~ \operatorname{He}_n(x)\operatorname{He}_n(y) </math>
Substituting <math>\rho = e^{-t}</math>, and letting <math>h_n := \operatorname{He}_n / \sqrt{n!} </math>, we have
<math display="block">\sqrt{\tanh(t/2)}\exp\left(-\frac{e^{-t} (x^2+y^2)- 2 xy}{4\sinh t}\right)
 = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (1-e^{-t})e^{-nt} ~ h_n(x)h_n(y) </math>

== Physics version ==
In physics, the [[fundamental solution]], ([[Green's function]]), or [[Propagator#Basic Examples: Propagator of Free Particle and Harmonic Oscillator|propagator]] of the Hamiltonian for the [[quantum harmonic oscillator]] is called the '''Mehler kernel'''.  It provides the [[fundamental solution]]<ref>[[Wolfgang Pauli|Pauli, W.]],  ''Wave Mechanics: Volume 5 of Pauli Lectures on Physics'' (Dover Books on Physics, 2000) {{ISBN|0486414620}} ; See section 44.</ref> <math>\varphi(x,t)</math> to 
<math display="block">\frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial^2 \varphi}{\partial x^2}-x^2\varphi \equiv D_x \varphi ~.</math>

The orthonormal eigenfunctions of the operator <math>D</math> are the [[Hermite polynomials#Hermite functions|Hermite functions]],
<math display="block">\psi_n = \frac{H_n(x)\, e^{-x^2/2}}{\sqrt{2^n n! \sqrt{\pi}}},</math>
with corresponding eigenvalues <math>(-2n-1)</math>, furnishing particular solutions
<math display="block"> \varphi_n(x, t)= e^{-(2n+1)t} ~H_n(x) e^{-x^2/2} .</math>

The general solution is then a [[linear combination]] of these; when fitted to the initial condition <math>\varphi(x,0)</math>, the general solution reduces to
<math display="block">\varphi(x,t)= \int K(x,y;t) \varphi(y,0) dy ~,</math>
where the kernel <math>K</math> has the separable representation
<math display="block">K(x,y;t)\equiv\sum_{n\ge 0} \frac {e^{-(2n+1)t}}{\sqrt\pi  2^n  n!} ~ H_n(x) H_n(y) \exp\left(-\frac{x^2+y^2}{2}\right)~.</math>

Utilizing Mehler's formula then yields 
<math display="block">{\sum_{n\ge 0} \frac {(\rho/2)^n}{n!} H_n(x) H_n(y) \exp\left(-\frac{x^2+y^2}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}} \exp\left(\frac{4xy\rho - \left(1+\rho^2\right) \left(x^2+y^2\right)}{2 \left(1-\rho^2\right)}\right)}~.</math>

On substituting this in the expression for <math>K</math> with the value <math>e^{-2t} </math> for <math>\rho</math>, Mehler's kernel finally reads
{{Equation box 1
|indent =::
|equation =  <math>K(x,y;t)= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sinh(2t)}}~\exp\left(-\coth(2t)~(x^2+y^2)/2 + \operatorname{csch}(2t)~xy\right).</math>
|border
|border colour = #0073CF
|bgcolor=#F9FFF7}}

When <math>t = 0</math>, variables <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> coincide, resulting in the limiting formula necessary by the [[initial condition]],
<math display="block">K(x,y;0)= \delta(x-y)~. </math>

As a fundamental solution, the kernel is additive,
<math display="block">\int dy \, K(x,y;t) K(y,z;t') = K(x,z; t{+}t')  ~.</math>

This is further related to the symplectic rotation structure of the kernel <math>K</math>.<ref>The [[quadratic form]] in its exponent, up to a factor of −1/2, involves the simplest (unimodular, symmetric) [[symplectic matrix]] in Sp(2,'''R'''). That is, 
<math display="block"> (x,y) {\mathbf M} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} ~,~</math> &nbsp; where
<math display="block"> {\mathbf M} \equiv\operatorname{csch} (2t) \begin{pmatrix} \cosh (2t) &-1\\-1&\cosh (2t)\end{pmatrix} ~,</math>
so it preserves the symplectic metric,
<math display="block"> {\mathbf M}^\text{T} ~ \begin{pmatrix}  0 &1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix} ~ {\mathbf M} = \begin{pmatrix}  0 &1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}  ~.</math></ref>

When using the usual physics conventions of defining the [[quantum harmonic oscillator]] instead via 
<math display="block"> i \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} + x^2\right) \varphi \equiv H \varphi,</math>
and assuming [[Quantum harmonic oscillator#Natural length and energy scales|natural length and energy scales]], then the  Mehler kernel becomes the [[Propagator|Feynman propagator]] <math>K_{H}</math> which reads
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\left\langle x \right| \exp (-itH) \left| y \right\rangle &\equiv K_{H}(x,y;t) \\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi i \sin t}} \exp \left(\frac{i}{2\sin t} \left (\left(x^2+y^2\right)\cos t - 2xy\right )\right ),\quad t< \pi,
\end{align}</math>
i.e. <math> K_{H}(x,y;t) = K(x,y; i t/2 ).</math>

When <math>t > \pi </math> the <math>  i \sin t </math> in the inverse square-root should be replaced by <math>\left|\sin t\right| </math> and <math>K_{H}</math> should be multiplied by an extra [[Lagrangian Grassmannian#Maslov Index|Maslov phase]] factor <ref>{{Cite journal|
journal=International Journal of Theoretical Physics|
date=1979 |
volume =18 |
issue = 4 |
pages= 245–250|
title= Extended Feynman Formula for Harmonic Oscillator|
author1= Horvathy, Peter  
|
doi=10.1007/BF00671761 |
bibcode=1979IJTP...18..245H |
s2cid=117363885 }}</ref>
<math display="block"> \exp\left(i\theta_\text{Maslov}\right) = \exp\left(-i\frac{\pi}{2} \left(\frac {1}{2} + \left\lfloor\frac{t}{\pi}\right\rfloor \right)\right).   </math>

When <math>t = \pi/2</math> the general solution is proportional to the [[Fourier transform]] <math>\mathcal{F}</math>  of the initial conditions <math>\varphi_0(y)\equiv\varphi(y,0)</math> since 
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\varphi(x,\, t{=}\tfrac{\pi}{2}) &= \int  K_{H}(x,y; \tfrac{\pi}{2}) \varphi(y,0) \, dy \\[1ex]
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi i}} \int e^{-i x y} \varphi(y,0) \, dy \\[1ex]
&= e^{-i \pi /4} \mathcal{F}[\varphi_0](x) ~,
\end{align}</math> 
and the exact [[Fourier transform]] is thus obtained from the quantum harmonic oscillator's [[Quantum harmonic oscillator#Ladder operator method|number operator]] written as<ref>{{citation |last1=Wolf |first1=Kurt B. |title=Integral Transforms in Science and Engineering |year=1979 |publisher=Springer}} ([https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-0872-1] and  [https://www.fis.unam.mx/~bwolf/integraleng.html]); see section 7.5.10.</ref> 
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
N &\equiv \frac{1}{2}\left(x-\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\right)\left(x+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\right) \\
&= H-\frac{1}{2}
= \frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}+x^2-1\right) ~
\end{align}</math> 
since the resulting kernel 
<math display="block"> \begin{align}
\left\langle x \right| \exp (-it N) \left| y \right\rangle &\equiv K_{N}(x,y;t) \\
&= e^{i t /2} K_{H}(x,y; t) \\
&= e^{i t /2} K(x,y;i t /2)
\end{align}</math> 
also compensates for the [[phase factor]] still arising in <math>K_{H}</math> and <math>K</math>, i.e. 
<math display="block">\varphi(x, \, t{=}\tfrac{\pi}{2})= \int K_{N}(x,y; \pi/2) \varphi(y,0) dy = \mathcal{F}[\varphi_0](x)~,</math>
which shows that the [[Quantum harmonic oscillator#Ladder operator method|number operator]] can be interpreted via the Mehler kernel as the [[Symmetry in quantum mechanics|generator]] of [[#Fractional Fourier transform|fractional Fourier transforms]] for arbitrary values of <math>t</math>, and of the conventional [[Fourier transform]] <math>\mathcal{F}</math> for the particular value <math>t = \pi/2</math>, with the Mehler kernel providing an [[Active and passive transformation#In abstract vector spaces|active transform]], while the corresponding passive transform is already embedded in the [[Bra–ket notation#The unit operator|basis change]] from position to [[Momentum operator#Fourier transform|momentum space]]. The eigenfunctions of <math> N</math> are the usual [[Hermite polynomials#Hermite functions|Hermite functions]] <math>\psi_n(x)</math> which are therefore also [[Fourier transform#Eigenfunctions|Eigenfunctions]] of <math>\mathcal{F}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|
journal=Symmetry |
date=2021 |
volume =13 |
issue = 5 |
title=Hermite Functions and Fourier Series |
author1= Celeghini, Enrico | 
author2= Gadella, Manuel |
author3= del Olmo, Mariano A. |
page=853 | 
doi = 10.3390/sym13050853 |
arxiv=2007.10406 |
bibcode=2021Symm...13..853C |
doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Proofs ==
There are many proofs of the formula.

The formula is a special case of the [[Laguerre polynomials#Hardy–Hille formula|Hardy–Hille formula]], using the fact that the Hermite polynomials are a special case of the [[associated Laguerre polynomials]]:<math display="block">\begin{align}
H_{2n}(x)   &= \left(-1\right)^n 2^{2n}   n!   L_n^{(-1/2)} (x^2) \\[4pt]
H_{2n+1}(x) &= \left(-1\right)^n 2^{2n+1} n! x L_n^{(1/2)} (x^2)
\end{align}</math>The formula is a special case of the [[Hermite polynomials#Kibble–Slepian formula|Kibble–Slepian formula]], so any proof of it immediately yields of proof of the Mehler formula.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ismail |first=Mourad E. H. |last2=Zhang |first2=Ruiming |date=2017-04-01 |title=A review of multivariate orthogonal polynomials |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1110256X16300761#bib0028 |journal=Journal of the Egyptian Mathematical Society |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=91–110 |doi=10.1016/j.joems.2016.11.001 |issn=1110-256X |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Foata gave a [[combinatorial proof]] of the formula.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Foata |first=Dominique |date=1978-05-01 |title=A combinatorial proof of the Mehler formula |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0097316578900663 |journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A |volume=24 |issue=3 |pages=367–376 |doi=10.1016/0097-3165(78)90066-3 |issn=0097-3165|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

[[G. H. Hardy|Hardy]] gave a simple proof by the Fourier integral representation of Hermite polynomials.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Watson |first=G. N. |date=July 1933 |title=Notes on Generating Functions of Polynomials: (2) Hermite Polynomials |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1112/jlms/s1-8.3.194 |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=s1-8 |issue=3 |pages=194–199 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-8.3.194|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Using the Fourier transform of the Gaussian <math display="inline">e^{-x^2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{ \pi}} \int e^{-t^2+2 i x t} dt </math>, we have<math display="block"> \begin{align}
H_n(x) &= \left(-1\right)^n e^{x^2} \frac {d^n}{dx^n} e^{-x^2} \\
&= \frac{e^{x^2}}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int \left(-2it\right)^n e^{-t^2+2 i x t} dt
\end{align}</math>from which the summation <math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(\rho/2)^n}{n!} \mathit{H}_n(x)\mathit{H}_n(y)  </math> converts to a double integral over a summation<math display="block">\frac{e^{x^2+y^2}}{\pi} \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-\left(t^2+s^2\right)+2 i (x t + y s)} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\left(- 2 t s\rho\right)^n}{n!} dt \, ds</math>which can be evaluated directly as two [[Gaussian integral]]s.

== Probability version ==
The result of Mehler can also be linked to probability. For this, the variables should be rescaled as <math>x \to x/\sqrt{2}</math>, <math>y \to y/\sqrt{2}</math>, so as to change from the "physicist's" Hermite polynomials <math>H(\cdot)</math> (with weight function <math>e^{-x^2}</math>) to "probabilist's" Hermite polynomials <math>\operatorname{He}(\cdot)</math> (with weight function <math>\exp(-x^2/2)</math>). They satisfy<math display="block">\begin{align}
H_n(x) &= 2^\frac{n}{2} \operatorname{He}_n\left(\sqrt{2} \,x\right), &
\operatorname{He}_n(x) &=2^{-\frac{n}{2}} H_n{\left(\frac {x}{\sqrt 2} \right)}.
\end{align}</math>Then, <math>E</math> becomes
<math display="block"> 
\frac 1{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\rho^2 \left(x^2+y^2\right) - 2\rho xy}{2 \left(1-\rho^2\right)}\right)
 = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\rho^n}{n!} ~ \operatorname{He}_n(x)\operatorname{He}_n(y) ~.</math>

The left-hand side here is <math>p(x,y)/p(x)p(y)</math> where <math>p(x,y)</math> is the [[Multivariate normal distribution#Non-degenerate case|bivariate Gaussian probability density]] function for variables <math>x,y</math> having zero means and unit variances: 
<math display="block">p(x,y) =
\frac 1{2\pi \sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\exp\left(-\frac{(x^2+y^2)- 2\rho xy}{2(1-\rho^2)}\right) ~,
</math>
and <math>p(x), p(y)</math> are the corresponding probability densities of <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> (both standard normal).

There follows the usually quoted form of the result (Kibble 1945)<ref name="Kibble">{{Cite journal
| last1=Kibble | first1=W. F.
| title=An extension of a theorem of Mehler's on Hermite polynomials
| doi=10.1017/S0305004100022313
| mr=0012728
| date=1945
| journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]]
| volume=41
| issue=1
| pages=12–15| bibcode=1945PCPS...41...12K | s2cid=121931906}}</ref>
<math display="block">p(x,y) = p(x) p(y)\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\rho^n}{n!} ~ \operatorname{He}_n(x)\operatorname{He}_n(y) ~.</math>

The exponent can be written in a more symmetric form:<math display="block"> 
\frac 1{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\exp\left(\frac{\rho(x+y)^2}{4(1+\rho)}-\frac{\rho(x-y)^2}{4(1-\rho)}\right)
 = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\rho^n}{n!} ~ \operatorname{He}_n(x)\operatorname{He}_n(y) ~.</math>This expansion is most easily derived by using the two-dimensional Fourier transform of <math>p(x,y)</math>, which is
<math display="block"> c(iu_1, iu_2) = \exp \left(-\tfrac{1}{2} \left(u_1^2 + u_2^2 - 2 \rho u_1 u_2\right)\right).</math>

This may be expanded as
<math display="block"> \exp( -(u_1^2 + u_2^2)/2 ) \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac {\rho^n}{n!} (u_1 u_2)^n ~. </math>
The Inverse Fourier transform then immediately yields the above expansion formula.

This result can be extended to the multidimensional case.<ref name="Kibble"/><ref>{{Citation | last1=Slepian | first1=David | title=On the symmetrized Kronecker power of a matrix and extensions of Mehler's formula for Hermite polynomials | doi=10.1137/0503060 | mr=0315173 | year=1972 | journal=SIAM Journal on Mathematical Analysis | issn=0036-1410 | volume=3 | issue=4 | pages=606–616}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|
journal = Mathematische Zeitschrift |
date=1995 |
volume =219 |
pages=413–449 |
title=Symplectic classification of quadratic forms, and general Mehler formulas |
author= Hörmander, Lars |author-link=Lars Hörmander | doi = 10.1007/BF02572374|
s2cid=122233884 }}</ref>

Erdélyi gave this as an integral over the [[complex plane]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Erdélyi |first=Artur |date=1939-12-01 |title=Über eine erzeugende Funktion von Produkten Hermitescher Polynome |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01210650 |journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift |language=de |volume=44 |issue=1 |pages=201–211 |doi=10.1007/BF01210650 |issn=1432-1823|url-access=subscription }}</ref><math display="block">\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\rho^n}{n!} \operatorname{He}_n(x) \operatorname{He}_n(y) 
= \frac{1}{\pi t} \iint \exp \left[-\frac{u^2+v^2}{\rho} + (u+i v) x + (u-i v) y - \frac{1}{2}(u+i v)^2 -\frac{1}{2}(u-i v)^2\right]  du \, d v .</math>which can be integrated with two Gaussian integrals, yielding the Mehler formula.

==Fractional Fourier transform==
{{main|Fractional Fourier transform}}
Since Hermite functions <math>\psi_n</math> are orthonormal [[Fourier transform#Eigenfunctions|eigenfunctions of the Fourier transform]],
<math display="block">\mathcal{F} [\psi_n](y) = \left(-i\right)^n \psi_n(y) ~,</math> 
in [[harmonic analysis]] and [[signal processing]], they diagonalize the Fourier operator,
<math display="block">\mathcal{F}[f](y) =\int dx f(x) \sum_{n\geq 0} (-i)^n   \psi_n(x)  \psi_n(y) ~.  </math>

Thus, the continuous generalization for  [[real number|real]] angle <math>\alpha</math> can be readily defined ([[Norbert Wiener|Wiener]], 1929;<ref>[[Norbert Wiener|Wiener]], N (1929), "Hermitian Polynomials and Fourier Analysis",  ''Journal of Mathematics and Physics'' '''8''': 70–73.</ref>  [[Edward Condon|Condon]],  1937<ref>[[Edward Condon|Condon, E. U.]]  (1937). "Immersion of the Fourier transform in a continuous group of functional transformations", ''Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA''  '''23''', 158–164. [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1076889/pdf/pnas01779-0028.pdf online]</ref>),  the [[fractional Fourier transform]] (FrFT), with kernel
<math display="block">\mathcal{F}_\alpha = \sum_{n\geq 0} (-i)^{2\alpha n/\pi}   \psi_n(x)  \psi_n(y) ~.  </math>

This is a ''continuous family of linear transforms generalizing the [[Fourier transform]]'', such that, for <math>\alpha = \pi/2</math>, it reduces to the standard Fourier transform, and for <math>\alpha = -\pi/2</math> to the inverse Fourier transform.

The Mehler formula, for <math>\rho = e^{-i\alpha}</math>, thus directly provides
<math display="block">\mathcal{F}_\alpha[f](y) = 
\sqrt{\frac{1-i\cot(\alpha)}{2\pi}} ~ e^{\frac{i}{2} \cot(\alpha) y^2/2}
\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-i\left(\csc(\alpha) y x - \frac{1}{2}\!\cot(\alpha) x^2\right )} f(x)\, \mathrm{d}x \,. 
</math>
The [[square root]] is defined such that the argument of the result lies in the interval <math>[-\pi/2, \pi/2]</math>.

If <math>\alpha</math> is an integer multiple of <math>\pi</math>, then the above  [[cotangent]] and [[cosecant]] functions diverge.  In the  [[limit of a function|limit]], the kernel goes to a [[Dirac delta function]] in the integrand, <math>\delta(x-y)</math> or <math>\delta(x+y)</math>, for <math>\alpha</math> an  [[Even and odd numbers|even or odd]] multiple of <math>\pi</math>, respectively. Since <math>\mathcal{F}^2[f] = f(-x)</math>, <math>\mathcal{F}_\alpha[f]</math> must be simply <math>f(x)</math> or <math>f(-x)</math> for <math>\alpha</math> an even or odd multiple of <math>\pi</math>, respectively.
